newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore Airlines shares dive after poor half year.
newsitem.headline: Singapore Airlines shares dive after poor half year.

text.p: Shares in Singapore Airlines (SIA) tumbled more than seven percent on Monday after the national carrier turned in disappointing half-year results.
SIA reported a modest 7.2 percent rise in net profit to Singapore $560.5 million (US$397.5 million) for the six months to September 30, from S$522.7 million in the same period last year.
The news prompted a rash of profit warnings from analysts, several of whom said the airline's full-year net profit might fall year-on-year in the 1996/97 year ending March 31.
Some suggested SIA would not hit the S$1.00 billion-mark in 1996/97. It reported net profit of S$1.025 billion in 1995/96.
The half-year net profit was near the bottom of market forecasts, which had ranged from S$550 million to S$600 million.
SIA said group operating profit for the period fell 11.4 percent to S$467.6 million.
The net result was only saved by a contribution of S$122.7 million from the sale of aircraft and spare parts.
"We have to revise down our forecasts for the full year," said Lim Eng Hai, head of research at brokerage J.M. Sassoon. "The results were disappointing all round."
The research arm of local brokerage DBS Securities said it was cutting its recommendation on SIA's foreign share tranche to "reduce" from "accumulate", meaning investors should sell.
DBS Securities is part of Development Bank of Singapore Ltd, which like SIA, is roughly half-owned indirectly by the Singapore government.
By Monday's market close, SIA's foreign shares were down S$1.00 at S$13.00.
SIA's results statement said the airline had benefitted from an increase in passenger traffic that had helped push up group revenue by 4.6 percent to S$3.53 billion from S$3.37 billion.
It carried 5.93 million passengers in the six months to September 30, up 10.2 percent from the same period in 1995. Cargo rose 10.5 percent to 320,900 tonnes from 290,500 tonnes.
But the company said it had been buffeted by escalating jet fuel prices and the strength of the Singapore dollar, eroding its operating yield by 6.7 percent.
It also expected yields to continue to come under pressure during the second half of the year.

"While there may be some respite on the currency front, the direction of fuel prices in the second half is uncertain, as is the recovery of the cargo market," SIA quoted deputy chairman and chief executive officer Cheong Choong Kong as saying.

Analysts agreed that jet fuel prices would continue to be a problem for SIA, but said the main challenge would be increasing competition for passengers, particularly for those travelling economy class on the most popular routes.
"It's tough," said Neil Payne, head of research at ING Barings. "Some other carriers have been cutting fares and I don't see SIA being able to put up its prices to cover costs."
"Escalating costs and falling yields suggest the full-year will be difficult," he added.
Analysts noted that SIA said it would not be able to repeat in the second half the one-off gain it made from selling old aircraft and spares in the first half.
ING Barings now believes SIA's net will be around S$941 million for the year ending March 31, 1997, down eight percent from the year before.
Most previous forecasts showed a rise of 14 percent to around S$1.16 billion for 1996/97, the Estimate Directory shows.

Several other brokerages said they were planning to cut their full-year forecasts to around or slightly below S$1.00 billion, implying falls of between two and three percent, but said they were not yet ready to publish their forecasts.
